A1.justification: Both PDFs describe An Effective Theory of Bias Amplification. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching theory and experiments relocated or renumbered in v4.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments validating predicted group risks and bias amplification, plus CNN experiments on Colored MNIST, with repeated-run results in the appendices.

after.justification: V4 retains original synthetic and Colored MNIST experiments and adds Colored MNIST label-noise and model-width sensitivity results in Appendix P.

M1.justification: The classical and Gaussian-random-projection ridge-regression procedures remain unchanged, as does the default CNN architecture. The CNN-width sweep adds evaluation configurations; Appendix R supplies practical guidance without changing the analyzed learning procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions cover Gaussian-mixture regression with isotropic, diatomic, and power-law covariance, and binary Colored MNIST classification with randomly assigned colors. V4's additional experiments vary label corruption and CNN width within the retained task rather than introducing another dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: The comparisons remain pooled versus separately trained group models, with empirical outcomes compared against analytical predictions. Newly discussed works such as Mannelli et al. and Jain et al. are not added as experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix P adds controlled Colored MNIST protocols: varying label-noise ratio at fixed width 500, and varying penultimate-layer width with both noise probabilities fixed at 0.05, evaluated after 80 steps. The existing splits, metrics, optimizer, and synthetic sample sizes remain unchanged. Clarified training-budget wording does not establish that the earlier experiment's budget changed.

E4.justification: V4 adds two sensitivity analyses testing whether nonlinear CNN behavior corroborates the predicted effects of label-noise disparity and model size (Figures 11–12). These extend corroboration on an existing dataset; the extensive synthetic sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report synthetic experiments using five-by-five runs with range error bars, and Colored MNIST results using standard deviations over ten seeds. V4 applies the existing practice to its added experiments and displays uncertainty directly in Figure 3; v1 already supplied that uncertainty in Appendix I.

E6.justification: The Colored MNIST training trajectory in Figure 3 is replaced: its final EDD is approximately 0.38 in v1 and 0.49 in v4, without establishing a performance improvement. New Appendix P results show EDD generally increasing with noise ratio and ODD decreasing or plateauing with width while EDD persists. The synthetic plotted results are retained.

T1.justification: The principal decompositions and proofs are retained. V4 revises the hypotheses of power-law Corollary 2, now M.1, corrects the separate-ridge squared-norm penalty, and removes inappropriate pseudoinverse identities. Conversely, Appendix A Equation 23 drops the Dirac masses present in v1 Equation 32's spectral-measure definition, introducing a localized mathematical error.

C1.justification: The main contributions remain a high-dimensional theory of bias amplification and minority-group disparities. Section 1.1 now explicitly qualifies the phenomena in Sections 4–5 as largely empirical observations supported by agreement with theory, and the introduction acknowledges earlier mixture-based bias analyses when positioning novelty.

C2.justification: V4 substantially expands applicability boundaries: nonlinear-network extrapolation, the lambda=1/t approximation, extraneous versus spurious features, parameter-estimation difficulties, and the unexplained Colored MNIST EDD behavior. Appendix R adds practical interpretation and guidance. However, Appendix J's new blanket claim of strictly increasing bias under underparameterization overstates Corollary J.1, which includes a zero-bias branch.

D1.justification: Appendix K clarifies image dimensions, training-only label corruption, and the interpretation of one group epoch as 80 steps. Appendix P specifies the added sweeps' controls. Reported CNN hardware changes from Quadro GP100 to NVIDIA L40S. The existing architecture, optimizer details, and supporting implementation links remain available.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 and new Appendix C substantially position the work against Mannelli et al. and Jain et al., distinguishing model-size analysis, covariance assumptions, and analytical techniques. V4 also develops its relationship to double descent and random-feature limitations, and Appendix I explicitly acknowledges calculations shared with Strong Model Collapse.

P1.justification: V4 reorganizes the theoretical narrative around random projections, consolidates the classical-model material in Appendices D–F, and moves experimental setup passages into Appendix K. Related work, model motivation, empirical interpretation, and the conclusion receive substantial explanatory rewriting, beyond renumbering or additions of scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn with error bars, v1's separate Colored MNIST uncertainty display is removed, and new Figures 11–12 present the noise and width sweeps. Conference formatting, author layout, captions, and figure placement change, while the existing synthetic graphics retain their designs and plotted content.

improvement.justification: V4 improves the paper through closer prior-work comparisons, more specific applicability limits, and additional Colored MNIST checks, including acknowledgment of imperfect agreement. These gains strengthen interpretation and empirical support while the central analysis remains stable. New localized errors in Appendix A's spectral-measure definition and Appendix J's monotonicity interpretation temper, but do not outweigh, the improvements.
